parts.name: Body
parts.does: the dark box; the film lies on its curved rails

parts.name: Back
parts.does: closes the box; carries the frame wheel and the post the film turns round

parts.name: Front plate
parts.does: holds the lens, the shutter and the wheel; slides onto the body

parts.name: Shutter
parts.does: swings across to let light in for an instant; the rocker on top is its button

parts.name: Spool
parts.does: the film is wound onto it first; its knob is the big red one

parts.name: Wind knob
parts.does: the small green knob; winds each picture back into the film's shell

parts.name: Frame wheel
parts.does: turned by the film; the arrow on its blue dial goes round once for each picture

parts.name: Lens
parts.does: one plastic lens, 12 mm across; pressed in from the front

parts.name: Pinhole ring and disc
parts.does: holds the pinhole disc flat in the lens pocket, instead of the lens

parts.name: Pinhole disc
parts.does: a thin metal disc with a 0.25 mm hole: laser-drilled in the kit, or a piece of drinks can and a pin

parts.name: 35 mm film
parts.does: any 35 mm film in its standard shell

parts.name: Near ring
parts.does: a thin ring under the lens that sets it for 1.5 m, for close pictures and the lesson on focus

parts.name: Fit gauge
parts.does: a comb of slots and a key: print it first, once per printer, to tune the fit

parts.name: Lens gauge
parts.does: checks a lens's size against the pocket before it is fitted

parts.name: Test slab
parts.does: a two-hour print of the front plate's finest details, to try a printer before the long parts

steps.title: Spool in
steps.do: Slide the spool, big red knob up, into the round chamber on the right (seen from behind).
steps.check: The big red knob sits on top of the camera and turns.
steps.fix: Its plain end goes into the slot in the floor, the knob's neck into the slot in the roof.
steps.why: The spool, its shaft and its knob are one piece, because this is the part you turn hardest. A collar on its neck rides in a pocket inside the roof: when the back is on, the knob cannot come out.
steps.narration: Build step one. Take the spool, the part with the big red knob. Slide it, knob up, into the round chamber on the right, seen from behind. Its plain end goes into the slot in the floor, and the knob's neck into the slot in the roof. Check it: the big red knob sits on top of the camera and turns. The spool, its shaft and its knob are one piece, because this is the part you turn hardest.

steps.title: Wind knob in
steps.do: Slide the small green knob into the slot on the left.
steps.check: It turns. It only comes out backwards.
steps.why: This knob will turn the film's own spool. Its forked end fits over a bar inside the film.
steps.narration: Step two. Slide the small green knob into the slot on the left. Give it a turn. It turns, and it only comes out backwards. This knob will turn the film's own spool: its forked end fits over a bar inside the film. So the green knob winds each picture back into the film's shell, and the red knob is where the film starts.

steps.title: Frame wheel into the back
steps.do: Lay the back down, inside up. Hold the blue frame wheel with its dial just past the edge of the back. Lay its neck in the fork, then slide it toward the long round post until its teeth touch the end of the post.
steps.check: The wheel turns freely. It does not lift out of the fork.
steps.fix: It was not slid home: slide it 3 mm toward the edge, press it down into the fork, slide it back.
steps.why: The film will turn this wheel: its eight teeth sit in the holes along the film's top edge, and one turn of the dial is one picture. Below the wheel, the film slides round the post.
steps.narration: Step three. Lay the back down, inside up. Hold the blue frame wheel with its dial just past the edge. Lay its neck in the fork, then slide it toward the long round post until its teeth touch the end of the post. The wheel turns freely, and it does not lift out. If it does lift out, it was not slid home: slide it toward the edge, press it down into the fork, and slide it back.

steps.title: Close the dark box
steps.do: Press the back on until both ends click.
steps.check: Two clicks. The back does not pull off. Pinch the two pads and it does.
steps.fix: The frame wheel is not slid home or a knob is not fully in.
steps.why: A nub on a springy finger at each end comes up behind a bar on the body. A ridge all round the back sits in a groove: that keeps the light out. This is the dark box. Everything else goes on its front.
steps.narration: Step four. Press the back on until both ends click. Two clicks. Now try to pull it off: it stays. Pinch the two pads and it lets go. A nub on a springy finger at each end comes up behind a bar on the body, and a ridge all round the back sits in a groove to keep the light out. This is the dark box. Everything else goes on its front.

steps.title: Shutter onto its peg
steps.do: Lay the front plate face down. Drop the shutter onto the round peg near the top edge, with its rocker (the bar across its top) hanging over the edge.
steps.check: The rocker sits just outside the edge. The shutter swings and clicks.
steps.mistake: If it will not lie flat.
steps.fix: It is upside down: the rocker must stand up toward you.
steps.why: The peg is the shutter's pivot. The shutter's own rim is its spring: a tooth on the rim drops into three notches in the edge of the pocket it lies in.
steps.narration: Step five, and the front plate. Lay it face down. Drop the shutter onto the round peg near the top edge, with the rocker, the bar across its top, hanging over the edge. The rocker sits just outside the edge; the shutter swings and clicks. If it will not lie flat, it is upside down. The peg is the shutter's pivot, and the shutter's own rim is its spring.

steps.title: Aperture wheel onto its peg
steps.do: Pick the plate up and hold it flat. Drop the wheel onto the other peg, handle down through the curved slot.
steps.check: The handle sticks out of the front. The wheel clicks into three places.
steps.mistake: If the wheel will not lie flat.
steps.fix: Its handle is not in the slot.
steps.why: The wheel carries three holes of different sizes. Its rim is a spring too.
steps.narration: Step six. Pick the plate up and hold it flat. Drop the aperture wheel onto the other peg, handle down through the curved slot. The handle sticks out of the front, and the wheel clicks into three places. If the wheel will not lie flat, its handle is not in the slot yet. The wheel carries three holes of different sizes, and its rim is a spring too.

steps.title: Camera onto the plate
steps.do: Keep the plate flat. Lower the camera onto it, front down, a little high and a little to one side, until its four pockets drop over the plate's four feet.
steps.check: The camera lies flat on the plate. Nothing rocks.
steps.fix: Move it about a few millimetres. The feet drop in at one place only.
steps.why: Each foot has a hook underneath and a lip on one side. Each pocket is open at one corner only: that is the way in, and the only way out.
steps.narration: Step seven. Keep the plate flat. Lower the camera onto it, front down, a little high and a little to one side, until its four pockets drop over the plate's four feet. The camera lies flat on the plate and nothing rocks. If it rocks, move it about a few millimetres: the feet drop in at one place only. Each pocket is open at one corner: that is the way in, and the only way out.

steps.title: Slide the plate across
steps.do: Pinch camera and plate together and turn them over. Slide the plate sideways until it stops.
steps.check: The point on the plate's top edge is in line with the middle line on top of the camera.
steps.fix: It is not flat on the camera: go back one step.
steps.why: Now the lips on the feet are under the camera's skin. The plate can no longer be lifted off.
steps.narration: Step eight. Pinch camera and plate together and turn them over. Slide the plate sideways until it stops. The point on the plate's top edge now lines up with the middle line on top of the camera. If it will not slide, it is not flat on the camera, so go back one step. Now the lips on the feet are under the camera's skin, and the plate can no longer be lifted off.

steps.title: Slide the plate down
steps.do: Slide the plate down until it clicks.
steps.check: One click. Its top edge is level with the top of the camera.
steps.fix: Press the plate flat against the body while you slide.
steps.why: The hooks are home and a springy tongue has dropped behind a bump. To come off, the plate has to go up past the click, then sideways, then away: a knock cannot do all three.
steps.narration: Step nine. Slide the plate down until it clicks. One click, and its top edge is level with the top of the camera. No click? Press the plate flat against the body while you slide. The hooks are home and a springy tongue has dropped behind a bump. To come off, the plate has to go up past the click, then sideways, then away. A knock cannot do all three.

steps.title: Lens in
steps.do: Press the lens into the round pocket on the front, bulge outward, until it stops. (No lens? The pinhole ring goes here instead.)
steps.check: It sits level and stays in when you shake the camera.
steps.mistake: If it is loose or will not go in.
steps.fix: Tell whoever made the kit: the pocket is made for one size of lens.
steps.why: Three small ribs in the pocket squeeze the lens. Nothing else in the camera is held by a squeeze.
steps.narration: Step ten, the last one. Press the lens into the round pocket on the front, bulge outward, until it stops. It sits level and stays in when you shake the camera. Three small ribs in the pocket squeeze the lens; nothing else in the camera is held by a squeeze. If the lens is loose, or will not go in, tell whoever made the kit. Press the rocker: click. Slide the handle: three clicks. Done.

steps.title: Open the back
steps.do: Pinch the two pads, top and bottom. Lift the back off.
steps.check: The frame wheel comes away with the back.
steps.why: Do this in the shade, never in bright sun.
steps.narration: Loading the film. Find some shade first: never do this in bright sun. Pinch the two pads, top and bottom, and lift the back off. The blue frame wheel comes away with the back, so lay the back down somewhere safe, inside up. From here until the back is closed again, keep the film out of the sun. Next, the green knob goes into the film.

steps.title: Knob into the film
steps.do: Slide the small green knob out. Push its forked end into the hollow end of the film.
steps.check: Turning the knob turns the spool inside the film.
steps.fix: The other end of the film has a peg sticking out.
steps.why: The fork straddles a bar inside the film's spool.
steps.narration: Slide the small green knob out of the camera. Push its forked end into the hollow end of the film. Now turn the knob: the spool inside the film turns with it. Wrong end? The other end of the film has a peg sticking out. The fork straddles a bar inside the film's spool, so from now on this knob turns the film's own spool.

steps.title: Film into its chamber
steps.do: Slide film and knob in together on the left, the film's lip pointing to the middle.
steps.check: The film sits flat in its chamber.
steps.narration: Slide the film and the knob in together, on the left, with the film's lip pointing to the middle of the camera. Keep them together as they go in. The film sits flat in its chamber, and the green knob sits in its slot on top, just as it did before. If the film will not sit flat, lift it out and try again with the lip facing the middle.

steps.title: Catch the film's tip
steps.do: Turn the big red knob until the slot in its spool faces you. Pull the film across and tuck its tip into the slot. Give the big red knob one turn.
steps.check: The film is caught. It lies over the two curved rails.
steps.fix: Tuck it deeper and turn again.
steps.why: The film lies on a curve around the lens. That curve is why one simple lens can be sharp from corner to corner.
steps.narration: Turn the big red knob until the slot in its spool faces you. Pull the film across and tuck its tip into the slot. Give the big red knob one turn. The film is caught, and it lies over the two curved rails. If the tip slips out, tuck it deeper and turn again. The film lies on a curve around the lens: that curve is why one simple lens can be sharp from corner to corner.

steps.title: Close the back
steps.do: Close the back.
steps.check: Two clicks. Keep it shut until the film is out.
steps.why: The frame wheel's teeth press on the film's top edge. If they are not in the holes yet, the first turn of the knob drops them in.
steps.narration: Close the back. Press until you hear two clicks, one at each end. Keep it shut until the film is out again. The frame wheel's teeth press on the film's top edge. If they are not in the film's holes yet, do not worry: the first turn of the knob drops them in. From now on, the film is in the dark.

steps.title: Wind the film out
steps.do: Turn the big red knob the way the picture shows until it stops: about 25 turns for a film of 24 pictures, about 33 for 36. Then leave it alone.
steps.check: While you turn, the arrow on the blue dial goes round and round: the film is moving.
steps.mistake: If the arrow does not move.
steps.fix: Open the back in the shade and tuck the film in again. When the knob stops, stop: never force it.
steps.why: The knob's teeth lean one way: your fingers catch when you turn it the right way and slip the other way. You have wound the whole film out of its shell. Every picture you take will be wound back into the shell, where light cannot reach it.
steps.narration: Turn the big red knob the way the picture shows until it stops: about 25 turns for a film of 24 pictures, about 33 for 36. While you turn, the arrow on the blue dial goes round and round: the film is moving. If the arrow does not move, open the back in the shade and tuck the film in again. When the knob stops, stop. Every picture you take will be wound back into the shell, where light cannot reach it.

steps.title: Pick a dot
steps.do: Slide the handle on the front to a dot. The chart shows which one, for your film and the light.
steps.check: It clicks at each dot.
steps.why: The dot shows the size of the hole behind it. Each dot lets in about twice the light of the one before. When even the largest is too small for a snap, take a time picture.
steps.narration: Taking a picture, step one. Slide the handle on the front to a dot. The chart shows which one, for your film and the light. It clicks at each dot. The dot shows the size of the hole behind it, and each dot lets in about twice the light of the one before. When even the largest dot is too small for a snap, take a time picture instead.

steps.title: Aim
steps.do: Aim along the middle line on top: from the edge of the pad at the back to the point at the front. The picture fits between the two outer lines.
steps.check: Stand at least two big steps away from what you are photographing.
steps.why: Nearer than that and the picture is not sharp: the focus is fixed.
steps.narration: Step two: aim. Look along the middle line on top, from the edge of the pad at the back to the point at the front. The picture fits between the two outer lines. Stand at least two big steps away from what you are photographing. Nearer than that and the picture is not sharp, because the focus is fixed. Put what matters in the middle: it is sharpest there.

steps.title: Press the rocker
steps.do: Hold still. Press the raised side of the rocker flat, in one quick press.
steps.check: One click. Now the other side is up: that is the side to press next time.
steps.fix: The shutter is open: press it on down. (That picture will be too bright.)
steps.why: A window in the shutter passes the hole as it swings. A quick press lets light in for about one three-hundredth of a second. A slow press lets in more.
steps.narration: Step three. Hold still. Press the raised side of the rocker flat, in one quick press. One click. Now the other side is up: that is the side to press next time. If the rocker stops level, the shutter is open, so press it on down. A window in the shutter passes the hole as it swings: a quick press lets light in for about a three-hundredth of a second.

steps.title: Wind on
steps.do: Turn the small green knob the way the picture shows until the arrow on the blue dial has gone once round. Keep your other hand off the big red knob.
steps.check: The arrow points at its mark on the body again.
steps.fix: Stop and take your hand off the big red knob. Never force it.
steps.why: One turn of the dial is one picture's length of film, wound back into the shell.
steps.narration: Step four: wind on. Turn the small green knob the way the picture shows until the arrow on the blue dial has gone once round. Keep your other hand off the big red knob. The arrow points at its mark on the body again. If the knob is stiff, stop and take your hand off the red knob: never force it. One turn of the dial is one picture's length of film.

steps.title: Wind it all back
steps.do: After the last picture, keep turning the small green knob until the arrow on the dial stops moving. Then three more turns.
steps.check: The arrow no longer moves: all the film is back in its shell.
steps.narration: The film is finished. After the last picture, keep turning the small green knob until the arrow on the dial stops moving. Then give it three more turns. The arrow no longer moves: all the film is back in its shell, in the dark. Only now is it safe to open the back. If the arrow is still moving, keep winding; never open the back before it stops.

steps.title: Take the film out
steps.do: Open the back. Slide the film out with its knob and pull the knob off. Send it off with your developing card, or take it to any photo lab.
steps.check: The film's tip is inside the shell, or just peeping out.
steps.why: Any lab that develops 35 mm film can do it.
steps.narration: Open the back. Slide the film out with its knob and pull the knob off. The film's tip is inside the shell, or just peeping out. Send the film off with your developing card, or take it to any photo lab: any lab that develops 35 millimetre film can do it. Ask for scans, and keep the negatives. They are the originals.

steps.title: Get or make the disc
steps.do: Take the pinhole disc from the bag, or make one. Ask an adult to cut a square about 10 mm across from a clean drinks can with kitchen scissors, and to snip off its four corners. Lay it on card, press a pin into the middle to make a dent, then push just until the tip comes through.
steps.check: Hold it up to a lamp: one tiny round point of light, no tear.
steps.mistake: A tear, or a hole you can see without the lamp.
steps.fix: Make another. The edges of can metal are sharp: hold it by its flat sides.
steps.why: The best hole for this camera is a quarter of a millimetre across: only the very tip of a pin. Lesson 1 shows why. No heating, no knives: scissors, a pin and a piece of card.
steps.narration: The pinhole experiment. Take the pinhole disc from the bag, or make one. To make one, ask an adult to cut a square about 10 mm across from a clean drinks can with kitchen scissors, and to snip off its corners. Lay it on card, press a pin into the middle, then push just until the tip comes through. Hold it up to a lamp: you should see one tiny round point of light.

steps.title: Disc and ring in
steps.do: Leave the lens out (or push it out from behind with the front plate off). Lay the disc flat in the round pocket, hole in the middle, and press the pinhole ring in on top of it until it stops.
steps.check: The disc covers the hole in the floor of the pocket all round. The ring stands a little proud and does not wobble.
steps.mistake: If the disc will not lie flat in the pocket.
steps.fix: Snip its corners a little more.
steps.why: Same plate, same pocket: with the lens it is a lens camera; with the disc and ring it is a pinhole camera. To change back, lift the ring out with a fingernail and tip the disc out.
steps.narration: Leave the lens out. Lay the disc flat in the round pocket, hole in the middle, and press the pinhole ring in on top of it until it stops. The disc covers the hole in the floor of the pocket all round. The ring stands a little proud and does not wobble. Same plate, same pocket: with the disc and ring it is a pinhole camera. To change back, lift the ring out with a fingernail.

steps.title: Take a pinhole picture
steps.do: Set the large dot. Stand the camera on something steady. Hold the rocker level to open it, count, press it down. Then wind on.
steps.check: ISO 400 film. Sun: open and shut. Cloud: count 1. Shade: 3. Indoors by a window: 40.
steps.why: The pinhole lets in about 150 times less light than the large dot, so a picture is counted, not snapped. It is sharp at every distance, and a little soft everywhere.
steps.narration: Set the large dot. Stand the camera on something steady. Hold the rocker level to open it, count, then press it down, and wind on. With ISO 400 film: in sun, open and shut. Cloud, count 1. Shade, count 3. Indoors by a window, count 40. The pinhole lets in about 150 times less light than the large dot, so a pinhole picture is counted, not snapped.

checks.name: Light
checks.question: Does light get in?
checks.proves: With the back on and the shutter shut, no straight or bounced path lets daylight reach the film.
checks.headline: 21 closed-camera cases, 69 million rays: none reach the film.

checks.name: Fit
checks.question: Do the parts fit on a real printer?
checks.proves: Every joint still goes together, turns and holds when printed thinner or fatter than drawn.
checks.headline: Every joint rebuilt on 5 printers, walls 0.15 mm thin to 0.25 mm fat: nothing binds, every hold remains.

checks.name: Overlap
checks.question: Do any two parts share space at rest or on the way in and out?
checks.proves: Every pair of parts, in every shutter and aperture state, is apart.
checks.headline: No two parts overlap in any of the four states; every way in and out is free.

checks.name: Motion
checks.question: Do the parts collide as they move?
checks.proves: Every moving part can travel its whole way, with a perforated film in place, without touching what it must not.
checks.headline: 1,865 positions stepped, with a film in place: nothing collides.

checks.name: Print
checks.question: Will it print without supports, on an ordinary printer?
checks.proves: Every part stands on the bed, has no thin or free-standing feature left unexplained, and slices cleanly.
checks.headline: Yes: 9.3 hours and 117 g of plastic for one camera, 0.2 mm layers, no supports.

checks.name: Snap and click
checks.question: How does every click and latch feel?
checks.proves: Each click is firm enough to feel and light enough for a hand, from the finite-element springs and the cam shapes.
checks.headline: Rocker 2.3 N, dot 2.4 N, back 0.6 N, front plate 3 to 5 N: nothing needs more than about 5 N.

checks.name: Strength
checks.question: Will the springs and latches bend without breaking?
checks.proves: The parts that flex stay under the plastic's strain limit in use.
checks.headline: Latch fingers, the shutter's rim and the frame wheel's teeth stay under their strain limits; the wind knob is the part that breaks first if the other knob is held.

checks.name: Fall
checks.question: Does the front plate stay on in a fall?
checks.proves: The two-move front plate survives most drops; a knock cannot do up, sideways and away at once.
checks.headline: From 1 m, typical printer: the front plate comes off in 7 % of falls.

checks.name: Focus
checks.question: Is the picture sharp?
checks.proves: The lens, traced at each dot, makes the middle of the picture sharp on a postcard from near to far.
checks.headline: Set for 3.7 m; sharp from 1.3 m with the small dot, and at any dot from 2 m (two big steps); softer toward the ends.

checks.name: Exposure
checks.question: Which dot for which light, and how much does printer error matter?
checks.proves: Printer error in the holes and the shutter's spring stays inside what the film forgives.
checks.headline: Dots f/16, f/11, f/9.5; shutter about 1/322 s; ISO 400: sun small, hazy middle, cloud large.

checks.name: Pinhole
checks.question: How big should the hole be, and how long to count?
checks.proves: The kit's disc is close to the best hole, covers the port on every printer, and the counts expose the film.
checks.headline: Disc 0.25 mm at 28.9 mm (f/116); 85 % of the picture lit at the large dot; ISO 400: sun open and shut, cloud 1, shade 3, indoors 40.

checks.name: Film path
checks.question: What touches the film, and what does the turn behind the gate cost?
checks.proves: Nothing but the rails and the post touch the film's face, and the winding pull stays within what a hand and the film take.
checks.headline: Only the rails' margins and the post's band touch the film; the picture area is never touched.

checks.name: Sight
checks.question: Is the line of sight over the top free?
checks.proves: The aiming marks are not blocked by the rocker in either shutter state.
checks.headline: The line over the notch and the blade's top is free in both shutter states.

checks.name: Is it sound?
checks.question: Taken together, should the design work, and what only a print can show?
checks.proves: One page of the model's own numbers, regenerated from the results above.
checks.headline: Nothing printed yet; nine things only a printed camera can show (SOUND.md).

terms.means: The opening that sets how much light gets through; on this camera, one of three holes in the wheel.
The focal length divided by the width of the hole; each step up the row 8, 11, 16 lets in half the light.
The part that opens for an instant to let light onto the film; here a plastic blade on a peg, pressed by the rocker.
How long the shutter stays open; this one has a single speed, about a three-hundredth of a second.
A tiny hole that makes a picture without a lens, because light travels in straight lines.
A shaped piece of clear plastic or glass that bends the light from each point of a scene back to one point.
How far behind a lens a distant scene comes sharp; this lens is 32 mm.
Where the lens makes the picture sharp; fixed on this camera, set for 3.7 m.
How much light the film gets for one picture: the size of the hole times how long it is open.
A picture where the shutter is held open and you count, for light too dim for a snap.
How quickly a film reacts to light; ISO 400 needs half the light of ISO 200.
The light-tight metal can the film comes in (a cassette); the film is wound back into it after every picture.
One picture's piece of film, 36 x 24 mm, and the window it is exposed through.
The row of holes along each edge of 35 mm film, 4.75 mm apart; eight make one picture.
The blue wheel whose eight teeth sit in the film's holes, so its dial goes round once per picture.
Moving the film one picture along after each picture; here the green knob winds it back into its shell.
A bent path at a gap that air can pass but light cannot, because light travels in straight lines.
The developed film, light and dark swapped; it is the original from which scans and prints are made.
The chemical baths that turn the hidden change in exposed film into a picture you can see.
A joint held by a spring made from the part's own plastic, that clicks into place with no screw or glue.
One slice of a print, laid down as hot lines of plastic; these parts print in 0.2 mm layers.
Extra plastic a printer adds under parts that hang in the air; none of these parts need any.
How far a printed size may be from the drawn one and still work; every joint here is checked from too thin to too fat.
The two marks on top of the camera you aim along; the picture fits between the outer lines.
